profile.name: siguiriyas
profile.tagline: A solemn, tragic cante jondo palo defined by a complex Romani 12-beat compás.
profile.insight: Introduced to the dance stage by Vicente Escudero in 1940, siguiriyas moves through a complex 12-beat pulse born from early Romani and Andalusian roots.
profile.profile: Siguiriyas is one of the oldest and most profound palos of flamenco music, belonging to the cante jondo category. Distinctly Romani in origin, its music is characterized by a complex 12-count compás, rubato expression, and tragic themes of suffering, imprisonment, and death. Though originally an unaccompanied vocal and guitar art form, its solemn and ceremonious dance was first introduced by Vicente Escudero in 1940. Today it remains a cornerstone of profound flamenco performance across Andalusia.
profile.profile_long:
Siguiriyas, also known as seguiriyas, siguerillas, siguirillas, or seguidilla gitana, stands as a fundamental pillar of cante jondo, the deep and expressive style of flamenco. Unlike many other palos, siguiriyas is purely Romani (Calé) in origin. Emerging around the late 18th century, its historical roots trace back between Cádiz and Sevilla, with key focal points in Triana, Los Puertos, Jerez de la Frontera, and Sanlúcar de Barrameda. The earliest forms of siguiriyas were performed without musical accompaniment, akin to primitive tonás, and some historical accounts classify it as a baile de velorio. Over time, guitar accompaniment became standard, though the nuances of the cante make it one of the most difficult styles to interpret and accompany.

Musically, siguiriyas is normally played in the key of A Phrygian. Each measure, known as the compás, consists of 12 counts with distinct accents falling on the 1st, 3rd, 5th, 8th, and 11th beats. This rhythm can be conceptualized by inverting the amalgama of compases of the soleá, shifting from a 6/8 and 3/4 structure to a 3/4 followed by 6/8 pattern. Because this counting method presents challenges, practitioners often simplify it into 5 beats comprising three short and two long beats, or count it as a soleá starting on beat 8. Performers frequently utilize rubato, allowing singers to increase and decrease tempo dynamically for dramatic effect. Furthermore, the compás incorporates counter rhythms played by the guitar, palmas, or dancer's footwork to create interlocking patterns.

The lyrical content of siguiriyas is intensely somber and tragic, dealing with themes of imprisonment, the death of loved ones, human suffering, and religious reflections. A hallmark of the vocal style is the introductory 'Ay' sung as a melisma across multiple syllables. Traditionally, verses follow a 6-6-11-6 syllabic structure consisting of two short six-syllable lines, a longer eleven-syllable line, and a final six-syllable line, though emotional intensity frequently overrides strict formal metrics, leading to variations such as 7-7-11-7 and 8-5-11-6.

Regional variants reflect the personal stamps of legendary interpreters. In Cádiz, the cante by El Planeta is characterized by simplicity and a lack of ornamentation. In Triana, styles associated with Frasco el Colorao and La Niña de los Peines are notably more ornate. Other variants derived from or governed by the seguiriya compás include serranas, livianas, and cabales, the latter being siguiriyas performed in a major key.

While the tradition began primarily as a vocal and guitar art, the dance for siguiriyas was first introduced by Vicente Escudero in 1940. Unlike fast-paced folk dances, the siguiriyas dance is ceremonious, pausado, solemn, and strictly unornamented. Its performance structure typically features a musical introduction by the guitar and singer, followed by an entrada, a letra dictated by the singer, an escobilla, a second letra, a danced falseta, and a concluding escobilla performed by the dancer.

sections.origins_and_history: Siguiriyas dates back to the late 18th century as part of the cante jondo tradition in Andalusia, with origins firmly rooted in Romani (Calé) culture. Early forms were performed a cappella like tonás, later developing guitar accompaniment. Key historical figures like the 19th-century cantaor El Planeta and his disciple El Fillo shaped its early classics, while the 1922 Concurso de Cante Jondo in Granada helped preserve its archaic forms through performers like El Tenazas and Manolo Caracol.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Introduced by Vicente Escudero in 1940, the dance is solemn, ceremonious, and pausado, lacking external ornamentation. The formal progression moves from a guitar and singer introduction to an entrada, initial letra, escobilla, second letra, danced falseta, and a final escobilla. Footwork and counter-rhythms interlock with the compás.
sections.music_and_instruments: Played in A Phrygian with a 12-count compás featuring accents on beats 1, 3, 5, 8, and 11. It utilizes guitar, palmas, and dancer footwork. Vocals feature heavy melismatic expression, notably the 'Ay' introduction, and follow a flexible verse structure (traditionally 6-6-11-6 syllables). Rubato and tempo shifts are heavily employed for dramatic effect.
sections.costume_and_setting: Not described in detail in the sources, though historically associated with intimate performance settings, traditional cafés cantantes, and wake gatherings (baile de velorio).
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Embodying the quintessence of jondura and cante puro, siguiriyas addresses profound human suffering, tragic love, imprisonment, and death. Historically linked to wake settings and serious artistic presentations.
sections.notable_figures: El Planeta (credited with the oldest style), El Fillo, Frasco el Colorao, La Niña de los Peines, Vicente Escudero (who introduced the dance in 1940), Paco La Luz, Silverio Franconetti, Diego Bermúdez Cala ('El Tenazas'), and Manolo Caracol.
sections.regional_variants: Variants differ across Andalusian regions: Cádiz features simple, unornamented styles (El Planeta), while Triana offers highly ornate interpretations (Frasco el Colorao, La Niña de los Peines). Related styles governed by the same compás include serranas, livianas, and cabales (major-key siguiriyas).
sections.lineage: Derived from primitive tonás. It forms part of the core cante jondo alongside soleares and tientos, and shares rhythmic frameworks with serranas and livianas.

teaching.level_notes: Advanced due to rubato timing, emotional intensity, and complex compás structure.

music_profile.sound_description: A deep, agonizing vocal performance delivered with rubato flexibility, anchored by sharp guitar bass attacks, steady palmas, and intricate counter-rhythms.
